documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Yearly exam, 56M.

Interval: had the overnight sleep study in December and saw pulmonology again in early January. He says they told him he has obstructive sleep apnea on top of the hypoventilation and set him up with a CPAP machine; has been using it most nights since early February. Sleepier days are a bit better, fewer morning headaches, though he takes the mask off some nights. We have not received a letter or the study report.

Meds: metformin 1000 BID, lisinopril 20, atorvastatin 40 qhs, HCTZ 25. NKDA. Beer about 2 a night.

Exam: vitals as charted. Obese. Thick neck. Heart RRR, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft. Trace pitting edema at both ankles. Feet: monofilament intact, pulses palpable. Skin unremarkable.
PHQ-2 0.

A/P:
1. Annual. Vaccines up to date for now; colonoscopy 2029. Labs: CMP, CBC, lipids, A1c, UACR, zinc.
2. OHS with sleep apnea per patient, on CPAP. Records request sent to pulmonology today so the chart has the study.
3. T2DM: A1c pending. If still above 7, start the second-agent conversation in earnest.
4. HTN, hyperlipidemia: continue.
5. Hyperzincemia: level today.
RTC 4 months.

documents.title: Physical labs
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Kurt, labs from Tuesday. A1c 7.3. Zinc is back up to 144 after being normal in 2023, so this comes and goes; still no symptoms or obvious cause, and I'll keep checking it yearly. Triglycerides remain high and the LDL is about where it has been. Red blood count still on the high side, which is what pulmonology expected with the breathing problem. Kidneys and urine protein fine. Keep using the CPAP every night; that matters for the blood count too.

documents.title: Records follow-up
documents.author: MA
documents.body: Called pulmonology office re: records request faxed 3/11, nothing received. They had no request on file. Re-faxed release with cover sheet asking for 1/3/25 visit note and polysomnography report. Confirmed receipt by phone.

conditions.label: Severe obesity due to excess calories

results.test: Carbon dioxide partial pressure in Arterial blood
Oxygen partial pressure in Arterial blood

reports.text: Attended overnight in-laboratory diagnostic polysomnogram. Recording montage included EEG, EOG, chin and leg EMG, ECG, nasal pressure, oronasal thermistor, thoracic and abdominal effort belts and pulse oximetry. Sleep onset and architecture recorded; total sleep time adequate for interpretation. Respiratory events were predominantly obstructive apneas and hypopneas. Apnea-hypopnea index 25 events per hour. No central apnea pattern. Sinus rhythm on single-lead ECG. No periodic limb movement disorder.
PA and lateral views. Lungs clear. No consolidation, effusion or pneumothorax. Heart size within normal limits for technique. Mediastinal contours normal. Bones intact.

Full pulmonary function testing with spirometry, lung volumes and pre/post bronchodilator. Good effort and reproducibility. FEV1 and FVC proportionally reduced with a preserved FEV1/FVC ratio. Total lung capacity mildly reduced. No significant response to bronchodilator.
reports.conclusion: Mild restrictive pattern without significant bronchodilator reversibility.

documents.title: Pulmonology Follow-up
documents.author: pulmonology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE PULMONARY AND SLEEP MEDICINE — FOLLOW-UP NOTE
Visit date: 01/03/2025

Returns after his sleep study. Daytime sleepiness and morning headaches are worse than in July, and he now has trouble holding concentration at work. His wife reports loud snoring and that he sometimes gasps in his sleep.

Medications unchanged: metformin, lisinopril, atorvastatin, hydrochlorothiazide. NKDA.

Exam: BP 145/92, HR 88. BMI 36. Neck circumference 44 cm. Lungs clear. Pitting edema of the lower legs.

Arterial blood gas, room air: pH 7.32, PaCO2 58, PaO2 68, HCO3 29.
Chest x-ray today: unremarkable.
Pulmonary function tests today: mild restriction, no significant reversibility after bronchodilator.
Polysomnography 12/10/2024: obstructive sleep apnea, AHI 25 events/hour.

Assessment:
1. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome with coexisting obstructive sleep apnea. The mild restriction on PFTs is consistent with body habitus; no airway disease.
2. Severe obesity due to excess calories (BMI 36 with hypoventilation).

Plan: Start CPAP, auto-titrating 5 to 15 cm H2O, with a full-face mask; order sent to the durable medical equipment supplier. Download review at the next visit, and we will move to bilevel if hypercapnia does not improve. Weight loss and avoiding evening alcohol encouraged. No driving when drowsy.

Outside Pulmonary and Sleep Medicine

[Received 04/22/2025 after second request. Includes polysomnography report.]

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Here for DM follow-up but says the real reason he kept the appointment: a few times in the last couple of months, carrying groceries up the hill or hurrying up stairs, he gets a mild pressure in the middle of his chest. Doesn't go anywhere, stops a few minutes after he stops moving. Never at rest. No change in how far he can walk otherwise. No palpitations, no shortness of breath beyond baseline. CPAP going well.
O: Vitals as charted. Heart RRR, no murmur. Lungs clear. No JVD. Ankles with trace edema, unchanged.
ECG in office: NSR, normal.
A/P:
1. Exertional chest discomfort, relieved with rest, in a 56-year-old with diabetes, hypertension, lipids and a grandfather with an early MI. Resting ECG normal. Referred to cardiology for evaluation. Reviewed reasons to call 911 (pain at rest, lasting over 15 minutes, with sweating or breathlessness).
2. T2DM: labs to be drawn with cardiology or at next visit.
3. Continue all current meds.

documents.title: Cardiology appointment
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Cardiology can't see me until January 19. Is that ok to wait? Haven't had the chest thing since I saw you.

documents.title: RE: Cardiology appointment
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: That's reasonable as long as it stays the way you described: only with real exertion, mild, and gone within a few minutes of resting. If it happens at rest, lasts longer, or comes with sweating or shortness of breath, call 911. Ask to be put on their cancellation list.

documents.title: Cardiology Consultation
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE CARDIOLOGY ASSOCIATES — CONSULTATION
Date of service: 01/19/2026
Requesting: primary care

History: 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, obesity complicated by obesity hypoventilation syndrome on CPAP, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia and a hyperzincemia his primary care physician has been following for several years. He describes infrequent mild chest discomfort with exertion, not radiating, that settles with rest. His exercise tolerance has not changed. Denies breathlessness and palpitations.

Medications: metformin, lisinopril, atorvastatin, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily. No known drug allergies.
Family history: paternal grandfather MI at 62; father diabetes and hypertension.
Social: never smoker; daily beer; software developer.

Exam: BP 138/86, HR 78. BMI about 36. Regular rhythm, no murmurs, rubs or gallops. Lungs clear.

Labs today: hemoglobin A1c 7.2%, fasting glucose 156, total cholesterol 210, HDL 40, LDL 130, triglycerides 800.

Impression: Exertional chest discomfort with multiple risk factors. Stable pattern.

Plan: Exercise treadmill stress test. Continue current medicines. Risk factor control through primary care. Will forward results.

Outside Cardiology Associates

documents.title: Went to the ER Saturday
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Heads up, I ended up in the ER Saturday with my right big toe. Woke up Friday night and it was on fire, couldn't put any weight on it. This was two days after a wedding, a lot of beer and a steak. They stuck a needle in the joint and said it's gout. Gave me colchicine. Already a lot better this morning. Do I need to do anything?

documents.title: RE: Went to the ER Saturday
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Sorry to hear it, glad it's settling. Take the colchicine exactly as the ER wrote it, and stop it if you get diarrhea. Plenty of water, and go easy on beer for now. We'll request the ER records and go over gout prevention at your September visit. If the pain comes back or you get a fever, call us.

documents.title: Emergency Department Summary
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT PHYSICIAN NOTE — outside hospital
Date of service: 07/11/2026

Chief complaint: right great toe pain.

HPI: 57-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and class II obesity. Right big toe pain started suddenly the night before arrival and has escalated so he cannot bear weight. Two days ago he was at a wedding, drank heavily and had steak. No trauma. First episode.

PMH: type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, obesity, obesity hypoventilation syndrome, hyperzincemia.
Meds: metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg at bedtime, hydrochlorothiazide.
Allergies: NKDA.
Social: never smoker, 3-4 beers daily.

Exam: Temp 37.8 C. Right first metatarsophalangeal joint red, swollen and exquisitely tender; limited by pain. Remainder of the foot without wounds. Other joints normal.

Procedure: right first MTP arthrocentesis under sterile technique, small volume of cloudy fluid obtained. Tolerated well.

Results: uric acid 8.5 mg/dL, WBC 11,000, CRP 20 mg/L, ESR 45 mm/hr. Synovial fluid polarized microscopy: negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals.

Diagnosis: acute gouty arthritis of the right first MTP (podagra).

Disposition: discharged home. Colchicine 0.6 mg tablets: 1.2 mg now, 0.6 mg one hour later, then 0.6 mg twice daily until the flare resolves. Avoid alcohol and large meat meals. Hydrochlorothiazide can raise uric acid; follow up with primary care in 1 to 2 weeks to review.

[Received 08/04/2026 after records request.]
